US consumers are planning to cut back on spending:

The proportion of consumers planning to spend more on restaurants, bars, and take out over the next 6 months fell -2 percentage points in August, to ~24.5%, the # since September 2025.

US consumers expecting to spend more on health care services fell -3 percentage points in August, to ~19.5%, the lowest since September 2025.

This also marks the steepest monthly decline among the top 5 categories tracked by the Conference Board's Consumer Confidence Survey.

At the same time, just ~21.5% of consumers now expect to spend more on beauty and personal care, down -1 percentage point from July and the lowest level since November 2025.

The US housing market is exceptionally weak:

The US Pending Home Sales Index fell -2.3% MoM in July, to 71.2 points, the # on record.

The gauge has collapsed -36% since July 2021 and remains down -33% from pre-pandemic levels.

Last month’s weakness was broad-based, with all 4 major US regions posting monthly declines.

The West recorded the steepest drop, falling -7.7% MoM to an all-time low, now -47.4% below its July 2021 level.

The South, the nation's largest home-selling region, fell -2.2% MoM to its lowest level since January 2025, down -36.2% since July 2021.

At the same time, pending home sales in the Northeast decreased -2.0% MoM, down -31.2% over the last 5 years.

The world's major central banks have finally unwound most of their pandemic-era balance sheet growth:

The Federal Reserve’s total assets as a % of US GDP are down to 21%, the lowest percentage since the 2020 pandemic.

By comparison, the peak was recorded in 2021 at ~37%.

At the same time, European Central Bank assets as a % of Eurozone GDP fell below 40% for the first time since Q1 2020, from the ~65% peak in 2022.

Total assets on the Bank of Japan’s balance sheet as a % of Japanese GDP are down to ~103%, their lowest since 2020, from the ~130% high in 2021.

The Bank of England’s assets are down to ~21% of UK GDP, the lowest since 2016, from the ~40% peak in 2021.

Energy stocks have rarely seen this much hedge fund demand:

Hedge funds bought the most global energy stocks in almost 4 years last week.

This also marks their 12th weekly purchase over the last 13 weeks.

As a result, hedge funds are now the most overweight energy relative to global stocks since June 2024.

This marks a sharp reversal from their most underweight positioning since 2021, recorded in February 2026.

The only period where hedge funds had a materially larger energy exposure relative to global equities was during the 2022 energy bull market.

The energy trade is becoming increasingly crowded.

Since Q2 2020, corporate profits have surged +$2.7 trillion, or +131%.

As a % of GDP, corporate profits jumped +1.0 percentage point in Q2, to 14.9%, an all-time high.

US companies are more profitable than at any point in history.
